lessons.title: Cell Structures and Microscopy
lessons.description: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, sub-cellular structures, light vs electron microscopy, magnification.
lessons.content_html:
Eukaryotic and Prokaryotic Cells

All living organisms are made of cells. There are two fundamental cell types you need to know: eukaryotic cells and prokaryotic cells.

Eukaryotic cells include animal and plant cells. They have a nucleus that encloses their genetic material within a nuclear membrane. They also contain membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria and ribosomes. Prokaryotic cells — such as bacteria — are much smaller and simpler. They lack a true nucleus; instead, their genetic material is a single loop of DNA floating freely in the cytoplasm. Prokaryotes may also contain small rings of extra DNA called plasmids.

Key Fact

Eukaryotic cells (animal and plant) have a nucleus that encloses their DNA. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no true nucleus — their DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm, and they may also contain plasmids.

Sub-cellular Structures and Their Functions

Both animal and plant cells are eukaryotic, but they contain different sub-cellular structures. Your exam requires you to explain how each structure's design relates to its function. This means you need to go beyond naming the structure — you must say why its shape, composition or position allows it to carry out its role efficiently.

Nucleus — contains the cell's genetic material (chromosomes made of DNA) and controls the cell's activities by determining which proteins are made. The nuclear membrane keeps the DNA separate from the cytoplasm, protecting the genetic code.

Cytoplasm — a jelly-like substance where most chemical reactions take place. Enzymes in the cytoplasm control these metabolic reactions. It also contains structural proteins that give the cell its shape.

Cell membrane — a thin, selectively permeable layer that controls which substances enter and leave the cell. It contains receptor molecules that allow the cell to respond to chemical signals.

Mitochondria — the site of aerobic respiration. They contain the enzymes needed for cellular respiration and transfer energy for the cell's processes. Cells with high energy demands (such as muscle cells) contain more mitochondria.

Ribosomes — tiny structures in the cytoplasm where protein synthesis occurs. They are found in both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, though they are smaller in prokaryotes.

Plant cells have all the structures listed above, plus three additional ones that reflect their roles in photosynthesis and structural support:

Chloroplasts — contain the green pigment chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis. They absorb light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose. Chloroplasts are found mainly in leaf cells and cells near the surface of stems, where light is available.

Permanent vacuole — a large, fluid-filled space containing cell sap (a solution of sugars and salts). It helps maintain the cell's rigidity by pressing the cytoplasm against the cell wall, keeping the cell turgid.

Cell wall — made of cellulose and surrounds the cell membrane. It strengthens and supports the cell, preventing it from bursting when water enters by osmosis. Unlike the cell membrane, the cell wall is fully permeable.

Key Fact

Plant cells have a cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts (photosynthesis) and a permanent vacuole (cell sap) in addition to the organelles shared with animal cells. Bacterial cells have a cell wall, but no true nucleus, no mitochondria and no chloroplasts.

Microscopy — Seeing Cells

Microscopes allow us to see cells and sub-cellular structures invisible to the naked eye. You need to know about light microscopes and electron microscopes and how to calculate magnification.

Light microscopes use glass lenses and visible light. They have a useful magnification of about ×1500 and a resolution of around 200 nm. To prepare a slide, place a thin sample on a glass slide, add a drop of stain (such as iodine or methylene blue) to make colourless structures visible, then lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles.

Practical work with light microscopes is a core assessed skill. You should be able to describe how to prepare slides, use staining techniques, and calculate magnification. Key steps:

1. Place a thin sample (e.g. onion epidermis or cheek cells) on a clean glass slide. 2. Add a drop of stain — iodine stains plant cell walls and nuclei yellow-brown, while methylene blue stains animal cell nuclei blue. 3. Gently lower a coverslip at 45° to avoid trapping air bubbles. 4. Start on the lowest magnification objective lens, focus, then switch to higher magnifications.

To calculate the total magnification: \(\text{total magnification} = \text{eyepiece lens} \times \text{objective lens}\). For example, a ×10 eyepiece with a ×40 objective gives ×400 magnification.

Electron microscopes fire a beam of electrons at the specimen. A transmission electron microscope (TEM) has much higher resolution — down to about 0.2 nm — and a magnification of up to ×2,000,000. This allowed biologists to see sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and the internal folds of mitochondria (cristae) in fine detail, greatly advancing our understanding of how cells work.

The development of electron microscopy was a turning point in biology. Before electron microscopes, scientists could see cells and nuclei with light microscopes, but could not resolve the detailed internal structure of organelles. Electron microscopy revealed that mitochondria have folded inner membranes (cristae) that increase the surface area for respiration enzymes — explaining why mitochondria are so efficient at energy transfer.

The magnification formula is: \(\text{magnification} = \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{real size}}\). Rearranged: \(\text{real size} = \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{magnification}}\).

Example: A cell appears 30 mm long in a diagram. The magnification stated is ×1000. What is the real size of the cell?
Real size = 30 mm ÷ 1000 = 0.03 mm = 30 μm.
Always convert to the same units before calculating. 1 mm = 1000 μm; 1 μm = 1000 nm.

Higher Tier: If a mitochondrion appears 8 mm long in an electron micrograph at ×40,000 magnification, its real length = 8 mm ÷ 40,000 = 0.0002 mm = 0.2 μm = 200 nm. This is just within the resolution limit of an electron microscope.

Key Fact

The magnification formula: \(\text{magnification} = \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{real size}}\). Always ensure both measurements are in the same units before calculating. Electron microscopes have much higher resolution (~0.2 nm) than light microscopes (~200 nm), allowing sub-cellular detail to be resolved.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 3-mark 'explain' questions about cell structures, always link structure to function — for example, 'mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, so cells with high energy demands contain more of them.' For magnification calculations, show your working and include units. A very common error is mixing millimetres and micrometres — convert everything to μm first. For 6-mark extended responses comparing cell types, use a structured approach: animal cells vs plant cells vs bacterial cells, naming specific organelles for each.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Eukaryotic cells (animal and plant) have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no nucleus — their DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm, and they may have plasmids.
  • Plant cells have three extra structures: cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts (chlorophyll for photosynthesis) and permanent vacuole (cell sap). Bacterial cells have a cell wall but no mitochondria, no chloroplasts and no true nucleus.
  • Light microscopes (resolution ~200 nm, magnification ~×1500) allow cells to be seen; electron microscopes (resolution ~0.2 nm, magnification up to ×2,000,000) reveal organelle detail. Magnification = image size ÷ real size.

lessons.title: DNA, Enzymes and Cell Division
lessons.description: DNA structure as a code, enzyme action, mitosis and the cell cycle, stem cells and differentiation.
lessons.content_html:
DNA — The Code of Life

Inside every cell is DNA, the molecule that carries genetic instructions for building and running an organism. DNA is a polymer — a long molecule made of repeating sub-units called nucleotides. It consists of two strands twisted around each other to form a double helix. The strands are held together by pairs of complementary bases: adenine (A) pairs with thymine (T), and cytosine (C) pairs with guanine (G). This is known as complementary base pairing.

The sequence of bases along the DNA acts as a code. Each group of three bases codes for a particular amino acid. This triplet code determines the order in which amino acids are assembled during protein synthesis at the ribosomes. Different sequences of amino acids produce different proteins, each with a unique shape and function.

Key Fact

DNA is a polymer made of two strands forming a double helix. The sequence of bases provides a code that determines the order of amino acids assembled into proteins at the ribosomes. Base pairs: A–T and C–G.

From DNA to Protein

The journey from gene to protein involves two key stages. First, in the nucleus, the relevant section of DNA is used as a template to produce a molecule of mRNA (messenger RNA). This mRNA carries the copied code out of the nucleus and into the cytoplasm. Second, at the ribosomes, the code on the mRNA is read and used to assemble amino acids in the correct order. The resulting chain of amino acids folds into a specific 3D shape, forming a functional protein.

Proteins are essential for life — they include enzymes (biological catalysts), structural proteins (such as collagen), hormones (such as insulin), and antibodies (part of the immune system). Because the DNA base sequence determines which proteins are made, DNA ultimately controls the cell's characteristics and functions.

Enzymes — Biological Catalysts

Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts, speeding up the chemical reactions that occur inside cells without being used up themselves. They play a central role in metabolism. Without enzymes, metabolic reactions would be too slow to sustain life.

Each enzyme has a uniquely shaped region called the active site. Only a substrate with the correct complementary shape can fit into the active site, like a key fitting into a lock. This is the lock and key hypothesis. When the substrate binds, the enzyme-substrate complex forms, the enzyme catalyses the reaction, and the products are released. The enzyme is then free to accept another substrate molecule.

Temperature — as temperature increases, molecules move faster and collide more frequently with the enzyme, increasing the rate of reaction. However, above the optimum temperature, the enzyme begins to denature — the bonds holding the active site in shape break, the active site changes shape permanently, and the substrate can no longer fit. The rate drops sharply. Different enzymes have different optimum temperatures — not all enzymes work best at 37°C.

pH — each enzyme has an optimum pH. For most human enzymes this is around pH 7, but pepsin in the stomach works best at around pH 2. Moving away from the optimum changes the active site shape, reducing activity. Extreme pH values cause permanent denaturation.

Substrate concentration — increasing substrate concentration raises the rate because more substrate molecules collide with enzyme active sites per unit time. Eventually, all active sites are occupied simultaneously (the enzyme is saturated) and the rate plateaus.

Enzyme concentration — more enzyme molecules mean more active sites available, so the rate increases (assuming excess substrate is present).

A common practical involves testing the effect of amylase on starch. Amylase is a digestive enzyme that breaks down starch into simpler sugars. Monitor the reaction by taking samples at regular intervals and testing with iodine solution — iodine turns blue-black when starch is present, but stays brown-orange once the starch has been fully digested.

To investigate the effect of temperature, set up water baths at different temperatures. Place test tubes containing amylase and starch in each water bath, allow them to equilibrate, then mix and start timing. Sample at intervals and test with iodine. Record the time taken for starch to be fully digested at each temperature.

To calculate the rate of reaction: \(\text{rate} = \frac{1}{\text{time}}\). A shorter time means a faster rate. Plot rate against temperature to find the optimum. Control variables include the volume and concentration of amylase and starch, and the pH of the buffer solution.

Key Fact

Enzymes have a specific active site that fits only one substrate (lock and key hypothesis). Above the optimum temperature or at extreme pH, the active site changes shape permanently — the enzyme is denatured and can no longer catalyse the reaction.

Mitosis and the Cell Cycle

Cells divide to produce new cells for growth, repair and replacement of damaged tissue. The cell cycle has several stages: first the cell grows and increases in size, then the DNA replicates so there are two copies of every chromosome, the cell grows a little more, and finally it divides by mitosis. Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell.

During DNA replication, the two strands of the double helix unzip. Each strand then acts as a template, with new complementary nucleotides added. The result is two identical copies of the original DNA molecule — one for each daughter cell. This ensures that genetic information is passed on faithfully during cell division.

Differentiation is the process by which a cell becomes specialised to perform a particular function. Specialised cells have specific structures suited to their role. For example, red blood cells are biconcave with no nucleus to maximise space for haemoglobin; nerve cells have long axons to transmit impulses over distance; root hair cells have extensions to increase surface area for absorption.

Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide and produce different cell types. Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into any cell type in the body — they are described as pluripotent. Adult stem cells (e.g. in bone marrow) can produce a limited range of cell types, such as blood cells. Meristems in plants contain stem cells that allow plants to continue growing and differentiating throughout their lives — unlike most animal cells, which lose the ability to differentiate early in development.

The use of embryonic stem cells raises ethical questions because the embryo is destroyed in the process. Some people argue the potential medical benefits — such as treating conditions like Parkinson's disease or diabetes — outweigh this concern. Others oppose it on moral or religious grounds. Adult stem cells avoid this controversy but have a more limited range of differentiation.

Key Fact

Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells for growth and repair. Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide to produce different cell types. Embryonic stem cells can form any cell type; adult stem cells have a more limited range.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For enzyme questions, 'killed' is always the wrong word — enzymes are denatured (active site changes shape permanently). For stem cell ethics questions, always present both sides: the medical potential versus the moral concern about embryo destruction. In the 6-mark extended response on cell division, make sure you describe the purpose of mitosis (growth, repair), the DNA replication step, and specify that daughter cells are genetically identical.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • DNA is a double-helix polymer. Its base sequence (triplet code) determines the order of amino acids in proteins. Base pairs: A–T and C–G.
  • Enzymes are biological catalysts with a specific active site (lock and key model). They are denatured — not killed — by high temperatures or extreme pH, causing a permanent change in the active site shape.
  • Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells during the cell cycle. Stem cells are undifferentiated and can produce specialised cell types — embryonic stem cells are totipotent; adult stem cells are more limited.

lessons.title: Respiration and Synthesis of Biological Molecules
lessons.description: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration, oxygen debt, and the synthesis of proteins, lipids and carbohydrates.
lessons.content_html:
What is Cellular Respiration?

Cellular respiration is a chemical process that occurs continuously in every living cell — animals, plants, fungi and bacteria all respire. It is not the same as breathing (ventilation) — respiration is a chemical reaction inside cells that transfers energy from glucose to a molecule called ATP. This energy drives all life processes, from muscle contraction and nerve impulse transmission to protein synthesis and active transport.

Respiration is an exothermic reaction — it transfers energy to the surroundings, which is why your body generates warmth. This transferred energy is vital: without it, cells could not carry out any of their functions.

Key Fact

Cellular respiration is a universal, exothermic chemical process that occurs continuously in all living cells. It transfers energy from glucose to ATP. It is NOT the same as breathing.

Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and occurs in the mitochondria. It produces a large yield of ATP, making it the most efficient form of respiration. This is why organisms with high energy demands (like mammals) rely primarily on aerobic respiration.

The word equation is:

$$\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} + \text{energy (ATP)}$$

The balanced symbol equation: \(C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O\)

Glucose is completely broken down in aerobic respiration. All the chemical energy stored in the glucose molecule is transferred — some to ATP for cellular work, and some as heat to the surroundings. This complete breakdown is why aerobic respiration releases much more ATP than anaerobic respiration.

Anaerobic Respiration

Anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen is not available or in short supply — for example, during intense exercise when blood cannot deliver oxygen fast enough to muscles. It takes place in the cytoplasm and produces much less ATP than aerobic respiration because glucose is only partially broken down.

In animal cells: \(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{lactic acid}\)

The incomplete breakdown of glucose produces lactic acid, which builds up in muscles during intense exercise, causing cramps and fatigue. After exercise, the body needs extra oxygen to break down the accumulated lactic acid — this is called the oxygen debt. You continue to breathe heavily after exercise to repay this debt: the extra oxygen is used to oxidise lactic acid in the liver, converting it back to glucose or carbon dioxide and water.

In plants and fungi (including yeast): \(\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{ethanol} + \text{carbon dioxide}\)

This process is called fermentation. It is used commercially in brewing (yeast produces ethanol for alcoholic drinks) and bread-making (yeast produces carbon dioxide that makes dough rise; the ethanol evaporates during baking).

The rate of respiration can be investigated using yeast in glucose solution or germinating peas. You can test for the products of respiration experimentally: breathing out through limewater turns it milky, confirming the presence of carbon dioxide. Using a temperature probe in a flask of germinating seeds or active yeast shows a temperature increase over time, confirming that respiration is exothermic.

For yeast fermentation, seal the flask with a bung connected to limewater via a delivery tube. As yeast respires anaerobically, carbon dioxide bubbles through the limewater, turning it milky. The rate at which this occurs can be compared across different sugar concentrations or temperatures.

Key Fact

Aerobic respiration (with oxygen, in mitochondria) produces a large yield of ATP. Anaerobic respiration (without oxygen, in cytoplasm) produces much less ATP. In animals it makes lactic acid; in fungi and plants it makes ethanol and carbon dioxide.

Synthesis of Biological Molecules

Respiration links to the synthesis and breakdown of key biological molecules. You need to understand the role of sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol as building blocks.

Carbohydrates: Simple sugars (monomers) such as glucose join together to form complex carbohydrates (polymers such as starch and glycogen). Glucose is the key monomer used in respiration. Starch is the storage form of glucose in plants; glycogen is the storage form in animals (stored in liver and muscles).

Proteins: Amino acid monomers join together in specific sequences (determined by DNA) to form protein polymers. Proteins are essential for enzymes, structural components (collagen, keratin), hormones (insulin) and antibodies. The sequence and type of amino acids determines the protein's shape and function.

Lipids: Formed from fatty acids and glycerol. Lipids are used for long-term energy storage (they contain more energy per gram than carbohydrates), thermal insulation, and making cell membranes. Lipids are not polymers in the strict sense because they are not made of repeating identical monomers.

The energy transferred by respiration is used both to build these molecules and to break them down. For example, energy from respiration drives the synthesis of proteins from amino acids, and the conversion of glucose to glycogen for storage. When the body needs energy, glycogen is broken back down into glucose for respiration.

Key Fact

Glucose monomers form starch (plant) or glycogen (animal) by polymerisation. Amino acids form proteins. Fatty acids and glycerol form lipids. Energy from respiration drives the synthesis of all these biological molecules.

Exercise and Respiration

During exercise, muscles need more energy, so the rate of respiration increases. The body responds by increasing heart rate (to deliver more oxygenated blood to muscles), increasing breathing rate and depth (to take in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide), and breaking down glycogen stored in muscles and the liver into glucose. If exercise is intense enough that blood cannot supply oxygen fast enough, muscles switch to anaerobic respiration, producing lactic acid. After exercise stops, continued heavy breathing supplies extra oxygen needed to break down lactic acid in the liver — this is the oxygen debt.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Never confuse respiration with breathing. For 3-mark 'explain' questions on exercise and respiration, link each adaptation to a reason: increased breathing rate → more oxygen delivered → aerobic respiration can continue. For extended responses on aerobic vs anaerobic, use the comparison table approach: location, oxygen requirement, products, ATP yield. In synthesis questions, always name the specific monomers (amino acids → proteins; glucose → starch/glycogen).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cellular respiration is an exothermic process in all living cells that transfers energy from glucose to ATP. Aerobic respiration (mitochondria, with oxygen) produces a large ATP yield. Anaerobic respiration (cytoplasm, no oxygen) produces a small ATP yield — lactic acid in animals; ethanol + CO₂ in plants and fungi.
  • Oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed after intense exercise to oxidise accumulated lactic acid in the liver.
  • Glucose monomers polymerise to form starch (plant storage) or glycogen (animal storage). Amino acids form proteins. Fatty acids and glycerol form lipids. Respiration provides the energy to build and break down these biological molecules.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Limiting Factors
lessons.description: Photosynthesis equation, limiting factors (light, CO2, temperature), interpreting rate graphs.
lessons.content_html:
What is Photosynthesis?

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and algae produce food. They are the main producers of biomass for life on Earth — almost all food chains begin with a photosynthetic organism. Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light energy.

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction — it takes in energy from the surroundings in the form of light. This is the opposite of respiration, which is exothermic. The word equation:

$$\text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{glucose} + \text{oxygen}$$

The balanced symbol equation: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{light}} C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\)

Photosynthesis is a two-stage process. In the first stage, light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll and used to split water molecules, releasing oxygen as a by-product. In the second stage, the hydrogen from water is combined with carbon dioxide to produce glucose. Both stages occur in the chloroplasts.

Key Fact

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction in chloroplasts: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\). Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll. It is a two-stage process: light splits water, then hydrogen combines with CO\(_2\) to make glucose.

What Happens to the Glucose?

Glucose produced by photosynthesis has several important uses in the plant:

Respiration — glucose is broken down to transfer energy for the plant's life processes. Starch storage — excess glucose is converted to insoluble starch for storage (starch does not affect osmosis because it is insoluble). Cellulose — glucose is converted to cellulose for building cell walls. Amino acids and proteins — glucose is combined with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil to make amino acids, which are assembled into proteins. Lipids — glucose can be converted to lipids (fats and oils) for energy storage in seeds.

Limiting Factors

Three main factors affect the rate of photosynthesis: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. Each can become a limiting factor — the factor in shortest supply that prevents the rate from increasing.

Light intensity — as light intensity increases, the rate increases because more energy is available for the light-dependent stage. At high intensity, the rate levels off because CO\(_2\) concentration or temperature becomes the limiting factor. The inverse square law applies: \(\text{light intensity} \propto \dfrac{1}{\text{distance}^2}\). Doubling the distance from a light source quarters the light intensity reaching the plant.

Carbon dioxide concentration — increasing CO\(_2\) provides more raw material for the carbon fixation stage, so the rate increases. Eventually, the rate plateaus when another factor (light or temperature) becomes limiting. In commercial greenhouses, farmers pump in extra CO\(_2\) to maximise crop yields.

Temperature — enzymes controlling photosynthesis work faster as temperature increases up to an optimum. Above this, enzymes denature and the rate drops sharply. Below the optimum, molecules have less kinetic energy and collide less frequently with enzyme active sites.

The three factors interact (Higher Tier). On a graph of rate vs. light intensity, you might see the rate plateau even though light is still increasing — this means CO\(_2\) or temperature is now the limiting factor. To increase the rate further, you would need to increase whichever factor is limiting. All three must be sufficient for the maximum rate to be achieved.

Key Fact

A limiting factor is the one in shortest supply that prevents the rate from increasing further. On a graph, it shows as a plateau. The three limiting factors (light, CO\(_2\), temperature) interact — all must be sufficient for maximum rate. The inverse square law: doubling distance quarters light intensity.

A common practical uses Elodea (pondweed). Place the pondweed underwater in a beaker with a lamp nearby and count oxygen bubbles produced per minute at different distances from the lamp. As the lamp moves further away, light intensity decreases (inverse square law) and fewer bubbles are produced, indicating a lower rate of photosynthesis.

For more accurate results, collect the gas in a gas syringe or measuring cylinder over water and measure the volume per unit time, rather than counting individual bubbles. Repeat each distance at least three times and calculate a mean to improve reliability.

You can also test leaves for starch using iodine solution: boil the leaf in water to kill the cells, then in ethanol to remove chlorophyll (the green colour), rinse in water, and add iodine. Blue-black = starch present (photosynthesis occurred). Brown-orange = no starch (no photosynthesis). This test can show which parts of a variegated leaf photosynthesise — only the green parts.

The inverse square law states: \(\text{light intensity} \propto \dfrac{1}{d^2}\), where d is the distance from the light source.

Example: A lamp is 10 cm from pondweed and the rate of photosynthesis is 40 bubbles/min. If the lamp is moved to 20 cm (double the distance), the light intensity drops to \(\frac{1}{2^2} = \frac{1}{4}\) of its original value. Expected new rate ≈ 10 bubbles/min.

This relationship is important when interpreting experimental results — a graph of rate vs. distance should show a curved decline, not a straight line. A graph of rate vs. \(\frac{1}{d^2}\) should give a straight line through the origin if light is the only limiting factor.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For limiting factor graph questions, always identify the plateau first, then explain which factor is limiting at that point and what would need to change to increase the rate further. For the 4-mark calculate question on the inverse square law, show the formula, substitute, and state the correct units. For the starch test practical, the sequence is: boiling water → ethanol → water rinse → iodine — getting the order wrong loses marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction in chloroplasts: CO₂ + H₂O → glucose + O₂ (using light). Light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll. Glucose is used for respiration, starch storage, cellulose, amino acids and lipids.
  • Three limiting factors control the rate: light intensity, CO₂ concentration and temperature. A plateau on a rate graph means another factor has become limiting. The inverse square law: light intensity ∝ 1/d².
  • Practical: Elodea bubble-counting (PAG B5) investigates the effect of light intensity. The iodine starch test shows where photosynthesis has occurred in a leaf.

lessons.title: Transport: Diffusion, Osmosis and Active Transport
lessons.description: Movement of substances in and out of cells, plus surface area to volume ratio for the challenges of size.
lessons.content_html:
Moving Substances Into and Out of Cells

Cells need to transport substances across their membranes to survive. There are three main mechanisms: diffusion, osmosis and active transport.

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration — it is passive (no energy needed). Oxygen diffuses into cells for respiration; carbon dioxide and urea diffuse out. The steeper the concentration gradient, the faster the rate of diffusion. Temperature and surface area also affect the rate — higher temperature means faster-moving particles and more frequent collisions.

Osmosis is specifically the movement of water molecules through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution (high water potential) to a more concentrated solution (low water potential). Osmosis is a special case of diffusion — only water molecules move, driven by the difference in water potential across the membrane. No energy is required.

Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient — from low to high concentration. This requires energy from respiration. Root hair cells use active transport to absorb mineral ions from the soil, where the concentration of minerals is lower than inside the cell. The energy comes from ATP produced by mitochondria in the root hair cells.

Key Fact

Diffusion and osmosis are passive processes (no energy needed, move down the concentration gradient). Active transport requires energy from respiration to move substances against the concentration gradient, from low to high concentration.

The classic osmosis practical uses potato cylinders placed in solutions of different sucrose concentrations. Cut cylinders of equal mass and length. Place one in distilled water, one in a low-concentration sucrose solution, one in a high-concentration sucrose solution. Leave for a set time (e.g. 30 minutes), remove, blot dry, and reweigh or remeasure.

In distilled water, water moves into the potato by osmosis (water potential of the potato cells is lower than the surrounding water), so the cylinder gains mass and becomes turgid. In a high-concentration sucrose solution, water moves out of the potato by osmosis (water potential of the sucrose solution is lower than the cells), so the cylinder loses mass and becomes flaccid or plasmolysed.

Plot a graph of percentage change in mass (y-axis) against sucrose concentration (x-axis). The intercept with the x-axis shows the isotonic point — where the water potential of the solution equals the water potential of the potato cells, so no net movement of water occurs.

A potato cylinder has an initial mass of 5.0 g. After being placed in distilled water for 30 minutes, its mass is 5.8 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass.

Percentage change = \(\dfrac{\text{change in mass}}{\text{original mass}} \times 100\) = \(\dfrac{5.8 - 5.0}{5.0} \times 100\) = \(\dfrac{0.8}{5.0} \times 100\) = +16%

A positive value means mass increased (water moved in by osmosis). A negative value would mean mass decreased (water moved out). Using percentage change rather than raw change in mass allows fair comparison between cylinders that had slightly different starting masses.

The Challenges of Size — Surface Area to Volume Ratio

As organisms get larger, their surface area to volume ratio (SA:V) decreases. Consider a cube: a 1 cm cube has SA = 6 cm², V = 1 cm³, SA:V = 6:1. A 2 cm cube has SA = 24 cm², V = 8 cm³, SA:V = 3:1. This means simple diffusion alone cannot supply enough substances or remove waste fast enough for large organisms. Multicellular organisms therefore need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems.

For a cube with side length l: SA = 6l², V = l³, SA:V ratio = 6l² ÷ l³ = 6/l.

Example: Calculate the SA:V ratio for cubes with sides 1 cm, 2 cm, and 4 cm:
1 cm cube: SA = 6 cm², V = 1 cm³, ratio = 6:1
2 cm cube: SA = 24 cm², V = 8 cm³, ratio = 3:1
4 cm cube: SA = 96 cm², V = 64 cm³, ratio = 1.5:1
As size doubles, SA:V ratio halves — larger organisms have a proportionally smaller surface area relative to their volume.

This is why a mouse loses body heat proportionally faster than an elephant — the mouse has a much higher SA:V ratio, so heat escapes more quickly relative to its body volume. It is also why single-celled organisms like amoeba can rely entirely on diffusion, while humans need a circulatory system.

Key Fact

As organisms get larger, their surface area to volume ratio decreases. This is why multicellular organisms need specialised exchange surfaces (e.g. alveoli in lungs, villi in the intestine) and transport systems to move substances efficiently. Single-celled organisms can rely on diffusion because their SA:V ratio is high.

Specialised Exchange Surfaces

Large multicellular organisms have evolved specialised exchange surfaces to overcome the limitations of a low SA:V ratio. These surfaces share common features: large surface area (to maximise the rate of exchange), thin walls (to minimise diffusion distance), good blood/fluid supply (to maintain steep concentration gradients), and in some cases ventilation (to maintain fresh supply of gases).

Alveoli in the lungs have a very large total surface area, walls just one cell thick, and a dense capillary network — all adaptations that maximise gas exchange. Villi in the small intestine have microvilli on their surface (brush border), increasing the surface area still further for absorption of digested food molecules into the blood.

Root hair cells in plants have long, thin extensions that greatly increase the surface area for absorbing water by osmosis and mineral ions by active transport from the soil. They contain many mitochondria to supply the ATP needed for active transport.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For osmosis questions, always use the correct term 'partially permeable membrane' and state the direction of water movement — from high water potential (dilute) to low water potential (concentrated). For SA:V ratio calculations, calculate surface area (all faces) and volume separately before dividing. A very common error is using raw change in mass rather than percentage change when comparing osmosis results across cylinders.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Diffusion: passive movement of particles down a concentration gradient (no energy). Osmosis: passive movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from high to low water potential (no energy). Active transport: movement against the concentration gradient, requires ATP from respiration.
  • As organisms get larger, SA:V ratio decreases — making diffusion alone insufficient. Large organisms need specialised exchange surfaces (alveoli, villi, root hairs) and transport systems.
  • Percentage change in mass = (change in mass ÷ original mass) × 100. SA:V ratio for a cube of side l = 6/l. Both are common calculation questions.

lessons.title: Plant and Animal Transport Systems
lessons.description: Phloem and xylem in plants, transpiration, blood vessels and the heart, plus the lung and digestive systems.
lessons.content_html:
Why Do Large Organisms Need Transport Systems?

Single-celled organisms can rely on diffusion alone to supply all their needs — their high surface area to volume (SA:V) ratio means diffusion distances are short. But as organisms get larger, their SA:V ratio decreases, and diffusion becomes too slow to supply oxygen and nutrients to cells deep inside the body, or to remove waste products efficiently. Multicellular organisms therefore evolved dedicated transport systems alongside specialised exchange surfaces.

Plant Transport — Xylem and Phloem

Plants have two types of transport tissue bundled together in vascular bundles: xylem and phloem.

Xylem vessels transport water and dissolved minerals upwards from roots to leaves. The cells are dead and form hollow tubes with thick walls reinforced with lignin, which makes them rigid and waterproof and provides structural support for the plant. Water moves through xylem as an unbroken column pulled upwards by evaporation from the leaves — this is the transpiration stream.

Phloem tubes transport dissolved sugars (mainly sucrose) from the leaves — where they are made by photosynthesis — to the rest of the plant, including roots, growing tips and storage organs. This process is called translocation. Unlike xylem, phloem cells are living and have sieve plates (pores) to allow the flow of sucrose. Translocation requires energy and can move substances both up and down the plant.

Key Fact

Xylem: dead hollow tubes reinforced with lignin; transports water and minerals upwards. Phloem: living tubes with sieve plates; transports dissolved sugars (sucrose) up and down by translocation. Both found in vascular bundles.

Transpiration

Transpiration is the evaporation of water vapour from the leaves through tiny pores called stomata. As water evaporates from the leaf surface, more water is drawn up through the xylem from the roots — creating the transpiration stream. Guard cells open and close the stomata: they become turgid (absorb water, swell, open stoma) in light, and flaccid (lose water, close stoma) in darkness or drought conditions.

Four environmental factors increase the rate of transpiration:

Light intensity — causes stomata to open wider, increasing water loss. Temperature — increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, speeding up evaporation. Wind/air movement — removes humid air from around the leaf, maintaining a steep concentration gradient for water vapour to diffuse out. Humidity — low humidity (dry air) increases the concentration gradient, speeding up water loss; high humidity slows it.

A potometer is used to measure the rate of water uptake by a plant cutting, which is taken as a proxy for the rate of transpiration. The distance moved by an air bubble in a capillary tube per unit time is recorded as conditions are varied.

The Human Circulatory System

Humans have a double circulatory system: one circuit pumps blood from the heart to the lungs for gas exchange (pulmonary circuit), and the other pumps oxygenated blood from the heart to the body (systemic circuit). This maintains high blood pressure for efficient delivery of oxygen and nutrients.

The heart has four chambers — two atria (receive blood) and two ventricles (pump blood out). The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body. The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall because it needs to generate higher pressure to pump blood around the whole body. Valves prevent backflow and ensure blood flows in one direction.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. They have thick, muscular walls with elastic fibres to withstand the surge of blood with each heartbeat. Their lumen (internal channel) is relatively small.

Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure. They have thinner walls and a larger lumen. They contain valves to prevent backflow and ensure blood moves only towards the heart.

Capillaries are microscopic vessels with walls just one cell thick, allowing efficient exchange of substances by diffusion between the blood and surrounding tissues. Oxygen and glucose diffuse out; carbon dioxide and waste diffuse in.

Red blood cells are biconcave discs with no nucleus, packed with haemoglobin to carry oxygen. Their biconcave shape increases surface area for oxygen absorption. White blood cells are part of the immune system — phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies. Platelets are cell fragments that help blood to clot at wound sites. Plasma is the liquid component of blood that transports dissolved substances including glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones, carbon dioxide and antibodies.

Key Fact

Blood flow through the double circulatory system: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. The left ventricle has thicker walls than the right because it pumps blood further.

Gas Exchange — The Lungs

The lungs are the site of gas exchange between the blood and the air. They contain millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli. Alveoli are adapted for efficient gas exchange with features that are the same as other exchange surfaces: very large total surface area, walls just one cell thick to minimise diffusion distance, moist inner surface to allow gases to dissolve, and a rich network of capillaries to maintain steep concentration gradients by removing oxygen and delivering carbon dioxide.

The Digestive System

The digestive system breaks down large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble ones that can be absorbed into the bloodstream. Key organs include the stomach (acid environment, protease enzymes break down proteins), the small intestine (enzymes from the pancreas complete digestion; products absorbed through villi into the blood), and the large intestine (water reabsorbed). The liver produces bile, which emulsifies fats (breaks large fat droplets into smaller ones, increasing the surface area for lipase enzymes to act on).

The inner wall of the small intestine is lined with millions of finger-like projections called villi, each covered in even smaller microvilli (the brush border). Together these massively increase the surface area for absorption. Each villus contains a dense capillary network (for absorbing glucose and amino acids into the blood) and a lacteal (a lymph vessel for absorbing fatty acids and glycerol from digested fats).

Villi share the same adaptations as other exchange surfaces: large surface area, thin walls (one cell thick), and a good blood supply to maintain steep concentration gradients. Glucose and amino acids are absorbed by a combination of diffusion and active transport; water is absorbed by osmosis.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For xylem vs phloem questions, remember the key distinctions: xylem is dead, lignin-reinforced, unidirectional (upward), transports water and minerals; phloem is living, bidirectional, transports sucrose by translocation. For blood vessel questions, structure always links to function: arteries have thick elastic walls for high pressure; veins have valves for low-pressure return; capillaries are one cell thick for diffusion. Never confuse atria and ventricles — atria receive, ventricles pump.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Xylem (dead, lignin-reinforced) transports water and minerals upwards by the transpiration stream. Phloem (living) transports sucrose by translocation, both up and down. Stomata control water loss — guard cells regulate their opening.
  • The human double circulatory system: heart (4 chambers, left ventricle thickest), arteries (high pressure, away from heart), veins (low pressure, valves, to heart), capillaries (1 cell thick, exchange surface).
  • Alveoli (lungs) and villi (small intestine) share common exchange surface adaptations: large surface area, thin walls, good blood supply. Both maximise the rate of substance movement by diffusion.

lessons.title: The Nervous System and Reflex Arc
lessons.description: How the nervous system, reflex arcs, synapses, brain and eye coordinate responses.
lessons.content_html:
Structure of the Nervous System

The human nervous system allows the body to detect changes in the environment (stimuli) and produce rapid, coordinated responses. It consists of the central nervous system (CNS) — the brain and spinal cord — and the peripheral nervous system — nerves that connect the CNS to receptors and effectors throughout the body (B3.1a).

The pathway for any nervous response follows a clear sequence: stimulus → sensory receptor → sensory neurone → CNS (relay neurone) → motor neurone → effector → response.

Key Fact

The nervous pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in CNS) → motor neurone → effector → response. The CNS (brain and spinal cord) processes information and coordinates the response.

Neurones and Their Structure

There are three types of neurone. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. Relay neurones are found within the CNS and link sensory neurones to motor neurones. Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands).

Both sensory and motor neurones share common structural features: a cell body containing the nucleus, short dendrites that receive incoming impulses, and a long axon that carries the electrical impulse away from the cell body. In motor neurones the long axon runs directly from the spinal cord to the effector. In sensory neurones a long dendron connects the receptor to the cell body, with a shorter axon entering the CNS. The axon is often surrounded by a myelin sheath, which insulates the axon and greatly increases the speed of impulse transmission.

Synapses

Where two neurones meet there is a tiny gap called a synapse. An electrical impulse cannot cross this gap directly. Instead, when an impulse arrives at the end of the pre-synaptic neurone, neurotransmitters are released from vesicles into the synaptic cleft. These chemicals diffuse across the gap and bind to specific receptors on the post-synaptic neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse that continues the pathway.

Synapses ensure impulses travel in one direction only, because neurotransmitters are released from one side and receptors are only present on the other. They also allow one neurone to connect with several others simultaneously, enabling complex coordination throughout the nervous system (B3.1b).

A reflex arc is the pathway that produces a rapid, automatic, protective response without conscious thought (B3.1c). The pathway goes: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector. Crucially, the signal passes through the spinal cord rather than the brain, making the response faster than a voluntary reaction.

For example, when your fingertip touches something sharp: pain receptors detect the stimulus → a sensory neurone carries the impulse to the spinal cord → a relay neurone connects directly to a motor neurone → the motor neurone stimulates arm muscles to contract → the hand is withdrawn. This protects the body from harm before conscious awareness of pain. Other reflex examples include the pupil reflex (pupils constrict in bright light) and the knee-jerk reflex.

Key Fact

Reflex arcs produce rapid, automatic responses that bypass the brain and pass through the spinal cord instead. This makes reflexes faster than voluntary responses and protects the body from injury before conscious thought.

The ruler drop test is a simple practical used to measure voluntary reaction time (B3.1c practical context, PAG B6). One person holds a ruler vertically at the 0 cm mark; the subject places their thumb and finger at the base without touching it. When the ruler is released without warning, the subject catches it as quickly as possible. The shorter the distance fallen, the faster the reaction time.

To improve reliability: repeat at least five times, discard anomalous results, and calculate a mean. Variables that could affect results include caffeine, fatigue, distractions and practice. This experiment measures a voluntary response rather than a true reflex — the information passes through the brain (visual cortex → motor cortex) rather than being processed in the spinal cord.

The Brain

The brain is the main coordination centre of the nervous system. It contains billions of neurones connected by synapses. Three regions are particularly important to know (B3.1d):

Cerebral cortex — the highly folded outer layer of the brain responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory, language and personality. The folding greatly increases surface area, allowing more neurones to be packed in. Different regions of the cortex are specialised — for example, the visual cortex processes information from the eyes, and the motor cortex controls voluntary muscle movements.

Cerebellum — located at the back of the brain. It coordinates balance, fine motor control and smooth, precise movements. Damage to the cerebellum results in loss of coordination and unsteady movement.

Medulla oblongata — at the base of the brain where it connects to the spinal cord. It controls involuntary, life-sustaining processes such as breathing rate, heart rate and swallowing. Because these functions are automatic, the medulla keeps them running without conscious thought.

Our understanding of brain function comes from several sources: studying patients with brain injuries, using electroencephalography (EEG) to record electrical activity, and modern MRI scanning to map active brain regions. However, the brain is enormously complex — many functions involve multiple regions working together, and some functions remain poorly understood. This makes treating brain disorders challenging.

The Eye

The eye is a complex sensory receptor for light (B3.1d). The key structures to know are: the cornea (refracts light), the iris (controls pupil size and therefore light entering), the lens (focuses light onto the retina), and the retina (converts light into electrical impulses via rod and cone photoreceptors). Impulses travel to the brain via the optic nerve.

Accommodation is the ability of the eye to focus on objects at different distances by changing the shape of the lens. To focus on a near object: the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments slacken, and the lens becomes fatter (more curved) to refract light more strongly. To focus on a distant object: the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments pull taut, and the lens becomes thinner (less curved), refracting light less.

Myopia (short-sightedness): distant objects appear blurred because the eyeball is too long or the lens too curved, causing light to focus in front of the retina. Corrected with a concave (diverging) lens. Hyperopia (long-sightedness): near objects are blurred because the eyeball is too short or lens too flat, causing light to focus behind the retina. Corrected with a convex (converging) lens. Both can now also be corrected with laser eye surgery, which reshapes the cornea.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions about the reflex arc often ask you to explain why it is faster than a voluntary response — the key point is that the signal does not travel to the brain, so fewer synapses are crossed and the pathway is shorter. For brain region questions, link each region to a specific function: cerebral cortex → consciousness and language; cerebellum → coordination; medulla → breathing and heart rate. For the eye, make sure you can distinguish between accommodation (ciliary muscles and lens shape changes) and the pupil reflex (iris muscles). ‘Explain’ questions need the mechanism, not just the outcome.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The nervous system coordinates responses via the pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (CNS) → motor neurone → effector. Synapses use neurotransmitters to pass signals in one direction only.
  • Reflex arcs bypass the brain and pass through the spinal cord, making them faster and protective. Three key brain regions: cerebral cortex (consciousness), cerebellum (coordination), medulla (heartbeat and breathing).
  • The eye focuses light via accommodation — the lens shape is controlled by ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments. Myopia (too curved/long eye) is corrected by concave lenses; hyperopia (too flat/short eye) by convex lenses.

lessons.title: Hormones, the Menstrual Cycle and Plant Hormones
lessons.description: Endocrine glands, menstrual cycle hormones, contraception, fertility, and plant hormones.
lessons.content_html:
The Endocrine System

The endocrine system uses chemical messengers called hormones to coordinate and control body functions (B3.2a). Unlike the nervous system, which produces fast, short-lived responses via electrical impulses, the endocrine system produces slower, longer-lasting and more widespread responses.

Hormones are released directly into the blood by endocrine glands and travel to their target organs. Only cells with the correct receptor molecules for a hormone will respond to it. Key endocrine glands include the pituitary gland (often called the “master gland” because it controls other glands), the thyroid gland, the adrenal glands, the pancreas, and the ovaries or testes.

Key Fact

The endocrine system uses hormones transported in the blood. Responses are slower but longer-lasting than nervous responses. The pituitary gland is the “master gland” that controls other endocrine glands.

Thyroxine (produced by the thyroid gland) regulates metabolic rate. It is controlled by negative feedback (B3.2b): when blood thyroxine is high, the pituitary gland reduces release of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), causing the thyroid to produce less thyroxine. When thyroxine is too low, the pituitary increases TSH output, stimulating more production. This loop maintains a stable metabolic rate.

Adrenaline (produced by the adrenal glands) triggers the “fight or flight” response in times of stress or danger. It rapidly increases heart rate, breathing rate and blood flow to muscles; it also stimulates the conversion of glycogen to glucose for extra energy. Unlike thyroxine, adrenaline acts very rapidly — it bridges the endocrine and nervous systems in speed of response.

The Menstrual Cycle

The menstrual cycle is controlled by four key hormones interacting through feedback mechanisms (B3.2c–d):

FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) — produced by the pituitary gland; stimulates maturation of an egg inside a follicle in the ovary and causes the ovaries to produce oestrogen. Oestrogen — produced by the ovaries; repairs and thickens the uterus lining after menstruation, inhibits further FSH production (negative feedback), and stimulates the release of LH. LH (luteinising hormone) — produced by the pituitary gland; a surge of LH around day 14 triggers ovulation (release of a mature egg). Progesterone — produced by the empty follicle (now the corpus luteum) after ovulation; maintains the thick uterus lining. If no fertilisation occurs, progesterone levels fall, the lining breaks down and menstruation begins.

Key Fact

The menstrual cycle is controlled by FSH (matures egg), oestrogen (repairs lining, triggers LH), LH (triggers ovulation around day 14) and progesterone (maintains lining). These hormones interact through feedback loops over the ~28-day cycle.

Hormonal contraception (B3.2e) includes the combined pill (oestrogen and progesterone), the mini-pill (progesterone only), implants and injections. These work by maintaining high levels of oestrogen and/or progesterone, which inhibit FSH production from the pituitary gland. Without FSH, no egg matures, so ovulation does not occur. Hormonal methods are highly effective but can cause side effects such as headaches, mood changes and, rarely, blood clots.

Non-hormonal methods include condoms (barrier method — prevents sperm reaching the egg and protects against sexually transmitted infections), diaphragms (barrier placed over the cervix), copper IUDs (create an environment hostile to sperm), and surgical sterilisation (permanent). Non-hormonal methods avoid hormonal side effects but vary in effectiveness. The choice of method depends on effectiveness, convenience, reversibility and whether STI protection is needed.

Hormones can also be used to help people who have difficulty conceiving (B3.2e, Higher Tier). FSH and LH are administered to stimulate egg maturation and ovulation in women who do not produce sufficient natural levels. In IVF (in vitro fertilisation), FSH stimulates the ovaries to produce multiple eggs; these are collected, fertilised outside the body, and the resulting embryos are implanted into the uterus. Success rates are moderate and the treatment can have significant physical and emotional impacts — these must be weighed against the personal benefit of achieving pregnancy.

Plant Hormones

Plants also respond to stimuli using chemical messengers. The two most important for the specification are auxin and gibberellin (B3.2e).

Auxin is produced in the growing tips of shoots and moves away from the tip. It promotes cell elongation — cells in regions with more auxin grow longer. When a shoot is illuminated from one side, auxin moves to the shaded side. Cells on the shaded side elongate more, causing the shoot to bend towards the light — a response called phototropism. This is advantageous because it maximises light capture for photosynthesis.

Rooting powders contain auxin. When cuttings are dipped in rooting powder, the auxin stimulates root growth at the cut end, allowing the cutting to establish quickly — useful for propagating plants commercially or in horticulture.

Weed killers (herbicides) exploit the fact that synthetic auxins at high concentrations disrupt normal plant growth. Broad-leaved weeds absorb the herbicide and grow uncontrollably, eventually dying. Narrow-leaved crop plants are less sensitive to the treatment, so the herbicide is selective.

Fruit ripening: ethene is a gaseous plant hormone that controls fruit ripening. Commercially, fruit is harvested unripe and stored in low-ethene conditions to slow ripening, then exposed to ethene gas to ripen quickly before sale. Gibberellins are used commercially to promote seed germination (for faster crop establishment) and to increase fruit size. Seedless grapes can be made larger using gibberellin sprays.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For menstrual cycle questions, be precise about which gland produces each hormone: FSH and LH come from the pituitary gland, oestrogen from the ovaries, and progesterone from the corpus luteum (the remains of the follicle). Mixing these up costs marks. For plant hormone questions, make sure you explain the mechanism not just the effect — don’t just say ‘auxin makes the plant bend’; explain that auxin promotes cell elongation and accumulates on the shaded side. ‘Evaluate’ questions on contraception or fertility treatments require you to consider both advantages and disadvantages.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The endocrine system uses hormones in the blood for slow, long-lasting, widespread responses. The pituitary gland (master gland) controls others. Higher Tier: thyroxine and adrenaline are regulated by negative feedback.
  • The menstrual cycle is controlled by four hormones: FSH (matures egg), oestrogen (repairs lining, triggers LH), LH (triggers ovulation day ~14), progesterone (maintains lining). Hormonal contraception inhibits FSH to prevent ovulation.
  • Auxin causes phototropism by accumulating on the shaded side of a shoot, promoting cell elongation and bending the shoot towards light. Plant hormones have commercial uses: rooting powders (auxin), selective weedkillers (synthetic auxin), fruit ripening (ethene) and germination promotion (gibberellin).

practice_questions.text: Name the gland that produces FSH and LH.
practice_questions.marks: Pituitary gland. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Describe how hormonal contraceptive methods prevent pregnancy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Hormonal contraceptives maintain high levels of oestrogen and/or progesterone (1), which inhibit FSH production so no egg matures and ovulation does not occur (1). Emerging: Vague — e.g. 'they use hormones to stop pregnancy' without explaining the mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain how auxin causes a shoot to bend towards a light source.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Auxin produced in the shoot tip moves to the shaded side of the shoot (1); it promotes cell elongation, so cells on the shaded side grow longer than cells on the lit side (1); the unequal growth causes the shoot to bend towards the light source (1). Secure: Two points with correct logic. Developing: States 'auxin makes cells grow' but does not explain unequal distribution. Emerging: Incorrect — e.g. 'auxin moves towards the light'.

practice_questions.text: A hormone is released by the pituitary gland around day 14 of the menstrual cycle and causes ovulation. Use the data below to calculate the mean LH level (mIU/mL) across days 13, 14 and 15: Day 13 = 18, Day 14 = 56, Day 15 = 24. Explain why the mean alone may not give a complete picture of the LH surge.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Mean = (18 + 56 + 24) ÷ 3 = 98 ÷ 3 = 32.7 mIU/mL (2 marks for correct working and answer); explanation that the mean obscures the sharp peak on day 14 — averaging smooths out the surge pattern which is clinically important for identifying ovulation timing (1 mark); any valid further point about variation/outlier effect (1 mark). Secure: Correct mean with partial explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how gibberellin is used commercially by fruit growers. Include the effect of gibberellin on plant growth in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Gibberellin promotes stem elongation and cell division, increasing fruit size (1); fruit growers spray gibberellin on grapes or other crops to produce larger fruit (1); gibberellin also promotes seed germination, allowing faster crop establishment (1). Secure: Two points. Developing: States 'it makes fruit bigger' with no mechanistic explanation. Emerging: Confusion with auxin or no agricultural context.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of hormonal fertility treatments such as FSH injections and IVF. In your answer, consider the benefits, limitations and ethical considerations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Benefits — FSH and LH stimulate egg maturation in women who do not ovulate naturally, enabling pregnancy that would not otherwise occur; IVF allows fertilisation outside the body and can be used when other treatments have failed. Limitations — success rates are not guaranteed and can be relatively low; treatment involves physical discomfort from hormone injections and egg collection; there can be significant emotional impact if treatment fails. Ethical considerations — multiple embryos are created and unused embryos are discarded or stored, raising questions about the moral status of embryos; there is debate about access and cost of treatment. A balanced, justified conclusion. Secure: Four points with some evaluation. Developing: Two benefits or two limitations without evaluation. Emerging: Single point with no structure.

Chemical substances produced by endocrine glands, transported in the blood, and affecting only cells with complementary receptors (target cells).
The speed at which chemical reactions occur in the body's cells, influenced by hormones such as thyroxine.
A control mechanism where a rising output inhibits further production, and a falling output stimulates production, keeping conditions within a narrow range.
